proposals.quote_modern: we made sure it had been the death of us
proposals.replacement: we felt sure it had been the death of us
proposals.butler: we made sure it had been the death of us
proposals.reader_evidence: Barrier ¶36 'we made sure it had been the death of us' (word, pause, high): read as 'we were certain it had killed us', with the note "'made sure' in the old sense of 'felt sure', not 'ensured'". Book-level note 2 lists "'made sure' for 'felt sure'" among the usages that read as early-20th-century British.
proposals.reason: False friend with a dead sense. In current English 'make sure' means 'ensure' or 'check', so the men's plea first reads as though they had ensured their own deaths. That is nonsense and forces a re-read, and the reader recovered only by recognizing the old idiom. Butler means 'we felt certain' (Greek 9.496 kai de phamen autoth' olesthai, 'and we thought we were lost then and there'). 'felt sure' keeps Butler's own 'sure' and is his own phrase for this sense elsewhere in the poem (PG #1727 line 9799, 'he felt sure it was Minerva'), so it restores rather than paraphrases (D29). 'had been' and 'the death of us' are unchanged. The meaning is recoverable from context, hence optional. Consistency note: accepted Book 4 prints Butler's 'made sure' unchanged twice (4.54, 4.57), where the 'ensure' reading is if anything more tempting ('we had made sure that it would come to nothing'). If the lead adopts this, those two belong to the same class; if the lead prefers edition-wide sameness, rejecting this one is defensible, because here the context forces the right reading.
proposals.collision_check: Butler's ¶36 has no 'felt' and no other 'made' or 'sure'. 'sure' is his own word here, in the same sense. Nothing else in the paragraph moves. Butler's 'felt' elsewhere in the Book (¶29 'felt about with his hands', ¶31 'felt the backs') is touching, in other paragraphs, and 'felt sure' is a fixed phrase that cannot be taken for touching. If the lead wants to keep 'felt' out of the Book entirely, 'we were sure it had been the death of us' is equally faithful and collides with nothing.

rejected_barriers.quote: King Alcinous
rejected_barriers.reason: Backstory, not a text defect (context note). Alcinous and the Phaeacian feast are set up in Books 6-8. Butler's name is kept.

rejected_barriers.quote: the cup-bearer draws wine and fills his cup for every man
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's syntax, kept almost word for word. 'for every man' says whose cup is filled, and the reader read it correctly with high confidence.

rejected_barriers.quote: so that you too may know it, and one day, if I outlive this time of sorrow, may become my guests
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's own logic: giving his name founds guest-friendship, so the hosts may one day be his guests. Butler and Homer leave it implicit. The reader drew the right inference, and spelling out the custom would add an explanation Butler lacks.

rejected_barriers.quote: renowned among mankind for all manner of subtlety
rejected_barriers.reason: Kept by prior rulings (task context): book09/continuity.md §7 (P002, i.e. ¶1, arrow C) restored Butler's own 'subtlety' because 'cunning' is Butler's word for Circe eleven words later in the same paragraph, and the 2026-09-23 accessibility screening declined the change again (citing findings-v1 M-2). The reader read 'cunning, cleverness and tricks' with high confidence, and the older sense of 'subtlety' (craftiness) is still in current dictionaries. No comprehension failure outweighs the ruling. If the lead ever overrides it, 'guile' collides with nothing in Butler's ¶1.

rejected_barriers.quote: Ithaca lies low on the horizon, farthest out to sea toward the sunset, while the others lie away from it toward the dawn
rejected_barriers.reason: The reader placed Ithaca correctly, westernmost of the group. 'lies low' renders Butler's 'lies squat', the recorded M-9 choice at the crux in Butler's footnote [48] (continuity §6). The apparent clash with the 'high mountain' is Homer's own, a low-lying island that has a mountain, and was not added by the modernization.

rejected_barriers.quote: my eyes know none they would rather look upon
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's construction ('my eyes know none that they better love to look upon'), with only the verb modernized. The island is the subject of the sentence, and the reader's reading, no place he would rather see, is right.

rejected_barriers.quote: the cunning Aeaean goddess Circe
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's epithet and name (GLOSSARY: Circe unchanged). Her story is told in Book 10. Unexplained names from elsewhere in the poem are not a defect (context note).

rejected_barriers.quote: bronze-shod spears
rejected_barriers.reason: A current, transparent compound, read correctly with high confidence.

rejected_barriers.quote: toward the time when men unyoke their oxen
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's time image, kept at the 2026-09-23 screening ('Butler's time images'). The reader read 'late afternoon' with high confidence.

rejected_barriers.quote: called three times upon each one of the poor fellows who had died
rejected_barriers.reason: The action is clear, and the reader described it correctly. The purpose of the rite is Homer's custom, left unexplained, and the edition adds no explanation Butler lacks.

rejected_barriers.quote: night came down out of the heavens
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's image ('night sprang forth out of the heavens'), read correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: We let the ships run before the gale
rejected_barriers.reason: A sailing idiom still in use, read correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: I should have got home unharmed then had not the north wind and the currents been against me
rejected_barriers.reason: 'should' for 'would' in a first-person conditional is dated but still grammatical. The reader resolved it with high confidence, and even read as 'ought to', the counterfactual 'had not the north wind ... been against me' keeps Butler's meaning. See recurring 'should'.

rejected_barriers.quote: they had a third man under them
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's phrasing. The reader read the rank relation correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: were for staying
rejected_barriers.reason: 'be for (doing)' meaning 'want to' is still current, and the reader read 'wanted to stay' with high confidence. Accepted Books 3 (3.13, 3.26) and 8 (8.45, twice) print Butler's idiom unchanged, so changing it here alone would split one idiom across the edition.

rejected_barriers.quote: made them fast under the benches
rejected_barriers.reason: 'make fast' (tie securely) is current, and the reader read it correctly with high confidence.

rejected_barriers.quote: without any kind of tillage
rejected_barriers.reason: A current word, read correctly with high confidence.

rejected_barriers.quote: their wild grapes yield them wine as the sun and the rain may bring them on
rejected_barriers.reason: The reader's real puzzle, how wine comes without winemaking, is Homer's content. 'bring them on' (make them grow) was read correctly. If the lead wants it plainer, D29 points to Butler's own 'as the sun and the rain may grow them'; Butler repeats 'grow' in this sentence himself, so restoring it collides with nothing. It is not needed for comprehension.

rejected_barriers.quote: sportsmen—who as a rule will suffer so much hardship in forest or among mountain precipices—do not go there
rejected_barriers.reason: 'sportsmen' for hunters is current, read correctly with high confidence. The dashed aside and the delayed reason are Butler's.

rejected_barriers.quote: no cables are wanted
rejected_barriers.reason: The reader read 'needed' with high confidence, and 'nor need a ship be moored' follows in the same sentence. 'needed' would render Butler's 'wanted' and his 'need' with one word in one sentence (collision rule, second clause), so the word stays.

rejected_barriers.quote: till the wind becomes fair for putting out to sea again
rejected_barriers.reason: 'a fair wind' is current nautical English, read correctly with high confidence.

rejected_barriers.quote: there were no breakers to tell us we were close in shore
rejected_barriers.reason: A current word, read correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: Here we came in
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's 'Here we entered'. As in Butler, the next paragraph confirms the island, and the reader identified it with high confidence.

rejected_barriers.quote: When Dawn, the rosy-fingered child of morning, appeared
rejected_barriers.reason: The GLOSSARY dawn formula (Book 2 table), fixed for every recurrence. The reader read it as sunrise, and Dawn as a goddess is Butler's.

rejected_barriers.quote: the nymphs, daughters of Zeus, roused the wild goats
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's content, read correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: Heaven sent us excellent sport
rejected_barriers.reason: 'sport' for hunting is current, read correctly with high confidence.

rejected_barriers.quote: the livelong day
rejected_barriers.reason: Kept by prior ruling (task context; 2026-09-23 screening). 'livelong' is current if poetic, and the reader read 'the whole day long' with high confidence. See recurring for the note on Book 10's different wording.

rejected_barriers.quote: the smoke of their stubble fires
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's own words ('the smoke of their stubble fires'); Homer has only smoke. The tension with ¶5 is Butler's, and the modern text must not correct him.

rejected_barriers.quote: loose the hawsers
rejected_barriers.reason: Kept by prior ruling (task context; 2026-09-23 screening). 'hawser' is current English, and the reader's reading, untie the mooring ropes, is right with high confidence.

rejected_barriers.quote: It was a station for a great many sheep and goats
rejected_barriers.reason: The edition's fixed noun (2026-09-23 screening). Butler's word. The reader read 'shelter or fold', which is right.

rejected_barriers.quote: a high wall round it made of stones built into the ground and of trees, both pine and oak
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's image, a wall of set stones and pine and oak trunks, read correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: resembling rather some crag that stands out boldly against the sky on the top of a high mountain
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's image, read correctly. That the Book never describes the Cyclops's body is Homer's content.

rejected_barriers.quote: a goatskin of sweet black wine
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's Homeric 'black wine' (dark wine), an image kept across the edition. Read correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: seven talents of fine gold
rejected_barriers.reason: The reader took it as a weight or sum of gold, which is right, and the list of gifts makes it a quantity. A gloss is not indispensable (brief: glosses only if indispensable).

rejected_barriers.quote: the wooded precincts of the temple
rejected_barriers.reason: Current, read correctly with high confidence.

rejected_barriers.quote: twelve jars of sweet wine, unmixed
rejected_barriers.reason: The custom is Homer's, and the next sentence shows it (twenty parts water to one). 'unmixed' is the edition's plain word for Butler's 'unblended'.

rejected_barriers.quote: I filled a large skin with this wine
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's (and Homer's) ring structure, returning to the goatskin after the Maron digression. The reader identified it correctly, and the modernization did not cause it.

rejected_barriers.quote: my mind misgave me
rejected_barriers.reason: Read correctly with high confidence ('I had a foreboding'). The familiar noun 'misgiving' keeps the verb transparent, and the word suits the edition's dignified register.

rejected_barriers.quote: lambs and kids
rejected_barriers.reason: Current farming words, read correctly with high confidence.

rejected_barriers.quote: first the yearlings, then the oldest of the younger lambs, and last the very young ones
rejected_barriers.reason: 'yearlings' is the recorded rendering of Butler's 'hoggets' (continuity §6), and it was read correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: all swimming with whey
rejected_barriers.reason: A current word, read correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: in the hope that he might give me a present
rejected_barriers.reason: The guest-gift custom is Homer's. Read correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: offered some of the cheeses in sacrifice
rejected_barriers.reason: The custom is Homer's. Read correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: let each of them have her own young
rejected_barriers.reason: Read correctly with high confidence.

rejected_barriers.quote: He curdled half the milk and set it aside in wicker strainers
rejected_barriers.reason: Current words, read correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: do you sail the sea as rovers, with your hands against every man and every man’s hand against you
rejected_barriers.reason: Read correctly with high confidence. The biblical ring is Butler's.

rejected_barriers.quote: We are Achaeans
rejected_barriers.reason: GLOSSARY keeps 'Achaeans'. The name comes from earlier Books, and 'on our way home from Troy' carries the sense.

rejected_barriers.quote: We are the people of Agamemnon, son of Atreus
rejected_barriers.reason: Backstory from other Books (context note). Read correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: we are your suppliants
rejected_barriers.reason: 'suppliant' is current (formal), and the reader's reading, formally begging protection under Zeus's law, is right. The custom is Homer's.

rejected_barriers.quote: Was it round the point, or is she lying straight off the land?
rejected_barriers.reason: Read correctly. 'she' for a ship is current.

rejected_barriers.quote: He said this to draw me out
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler and Homer leave the Cyclops's motive implicit. The reader inferred it correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: a drink of neat milk
rejected_barriers.reason: Kept (D29). 'neat' meaning undiluted is still current for drinks ('whiskey neat'), which is how the reader, though unsure, reached 'plain, undiluted milk'. Nothing in the story turns on it: Homer's point (9.297 akreton gala, milk taken unmixed) is a small detail, and a reader who takes 'neat' as 'plain' loses nothing that matters. Butler keeps 'neat' (milk, ¶18) apart from 'unblended' (wine, ¶11, printed 'unmixed'), so 'unmixed' here would merge two of his words in one Book. If the lead wants a change anyway, 'undiluted' merges nothing and collides with nothing in Butler's ¶18.

rejected_barriers.quote: as easily as though he were merely clapping the lid on a quiver full of arrows
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's image, read correctly with high confidence.

rejected_barriers.quote: milked his goats and ewes, all quite properly
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's 'all quite rightly' (Homer's 'all in due order'), read correctly. Any irony is Butler's own.

rejected_barriers.quote: green olive wood
rejected_barriers.reason: Read correctly with high confidence. The sentence itself says the wood must dry.

rejected_barriers.quote: a twenty-oared merchant ship of large burden
rejected_barriers.reason: A current nautical term, read correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: The lot fell on the very four I should have chosen
rejected_barriers.reason: See ¶3 and recurring 'should'. The reader resolved it with high confidence, and even read as 'ought to have chosen' it keeps Butler's point that the lot chose the best men.

rejected_barriers.quote: bore it into the monster’s eye
rejected_barriers.reason: Homer's content: the text never says the Cyclops has one eye (context note). Not a defect.

rejected_barriers.quote: some fancy must have taken him
rejected_barriers.reason: Read correctly with high confidence.

rejected_barriers.quote: as a drink offering
rejected_barriers.reason: The standard term (PUNCTUATION §4), read correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: ramping and raving intolerably
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's alliterative pair, read correctly ('raging and ranting').

rejected_barriers.quote: this drinks like nectar and ambrosia all in one
rejected_barriers.reason: Read correctly. 'ambrosia' is current.

rejected_barriers.quote: My name is Noman
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's device, kept exactly (continuity §6; task context). The reader caught the set-up with high confidence, and it pays off at ¶26-27 as in Butler.

rejected_barriers.quote: gobbets of human flesh
rejected_barriers.reason: Known item (9.25), kept. 'gobbet' (a lump of flesh) is current English, exact and vivid, and D29 keeps Butler's word. The reader read 'lumps of human flesh' with high confidence. The 2026-09-23 screening already declined 'chunks' as a change to Butler's words.

rejected_barriers.quote: boring a hole in a ship’s plank with an auger that two men with a wheel and strap can keep turning
rejected_barriers.reason: Already adapted at the 2026-09-23 screening, which applied the blocking finding (candidate-v4: 'an auger, which two men ... can keep on turning' became 'an auger that two men ... can keep turning'). The reader's picture, a drill spun by two men pulling a strap, is exactly Homer's image (9.384-386). The simile's point, steady turning, is carried by 'keep turning as long as they choose'. The tool is Butler's image and stays.

rejected_barriers.quote: all besmirched with gore
rejected_barriers.reason: Known item (9.25), kept. Round-1 finding M-5 restored 'besmirched' in place of 'besmeared' ('a current English word replaced by a rarer one, for nothing'; ACCEPTANCE, M-2 to M-8). The literal sense (soiled, smeared) is in current dictionaries, and 'with gore' fixes it. The reader read 'covered in blood' with high confidence.

rejected_barriers.quote: made the cave ring again
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's 'ring again' means re-echoed. A reader who takes 'again' as 'once more' loses only the echo, and the story is unchanged. The reader caught the old sense with high confidence. Kept here and at 10.37 ('rang again').

rejected_barriers.quote: We ran away in a fright
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's words, read correctly: they retreat inside the blocked cave.

rejected_barriers.quote: Even so did we bore ... even so did the Cyclops’ eye hiss
rejected_barriers.reason: Not flagged by this reader; known item, kept by prior ruling (task context; findings-v1 notes that the inversion keeps the correlative reading; 2026-09-23 screening). Both clauses answer 'as though I were boring ...' and 'As a blacksmith ...', and the reader's paraphrase ('twisting it like a shipbuilder's drill ... hisses like hot iron plunged into water') shows both similes landed.

rejected_barriers.quote: either by fraud or by force
rejected_barriers.reason: 'fraud' meaning deceit is current and is half of the Noman pun ('by fraud or by force'). Read correctly with high confidence.

rejected_barriers.quote: Noman is killing me by fraud; no man is killing me by force.
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's pun, identical in the modern text, and the reader's reading is exactly Butler's. That the two sound alike when read aloud is an audio or app matter. The capital letter is Butler's own device, and it must keep working (task context).

rejected_barriers.quote: felt the backs of all the sheep as they stood upright
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's words (Homer's 'standing upright'), read correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: got him down in his drink and blinded him
rejected_barriers.reason: The Cyclops speaks of himself in the third person to his ram, as in Butler. Read correctly with high confidence.

rejected_barriers.quote: you should have taken better measure of your man
rejected_barriers.reason: Read correctly with high confidence.

rejected_barriers.quote: flung it just in front of my ship, so that it came within a little of hitting the end of the rudder
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's (and Homer's) own inconsistency. Homer's 9.483 repeats 9.540, where the rock falls behind the ship. The modern text follows Butler exactly and must not resolve it.

rejected_barriers.quote: kept the ship off
rejected_barriers.reason: Read correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: they laid out with a will
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's rowing idiom. The order to 'row for their lives' comes just before it, and the reader read it correctly. The same ruling applies at 10.10.

rejected_barriers.quote: I was for jeering at the Cyclops again
rejected_barriers.reason: See ¶4: a current idiom, printed in accepted Books 3 and 8. Read correctly with high confidence.

rejected_barriers.quote: Come here, then, Odysseus, that I may make you presents to show my hospitality
rejected_barriers.reason: Homer leaves the trap unflagged, and the reader saw it anyway. Not a text defect.

rejected_barriers.quote: I wish I could be as sure of killing you outright and sending you down to the house of Hades, as I am that it will take more than Poseidon to cure that eye of yours
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's comparison, read correctly with high confidence.

rejected_barriers.quote: the firmament of heaven
rejected_barriers.reason: Read correctly with high confidence. The word suits the dignified register.

rejected_barriers.quote: in sore plight
rejected_barriers.reason: 'in sore plight' (in a wretched state) is literary but current, as in 'sore need'. Read correctly with high confidence.

rejected_barriers.quote: Poseidon heard his prayer. Then he picked up a rock
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's pronoun, unchanged ('Then he picked up a rock much larger than the first'). The reader resolved it with high confidence: 'much larger than the first' points back to whoever threw the ¶35 rock, and this rock falls short, as a god's would not. Naming 'the Cyclops' would be a one-word clarification, but no comprehension failure calls for it.

rejected_barriers.quote: toward the shore of the island
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's reference, confirmed in the next paragraph. Read correctly with high confidence.

rejected_barriers.quote: burned its thigh bones to Zeus
rejected_barriers.reason: The custom is Homer's. Read correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: But he took no heed of my sacrifice, and only thought how he might destroy both my ships and my comrades.
rejected_barriers.reason: Homer's content: Zeus rejecting the ram (context note). Homer leaves the link to Poseidon's anger implicit.

rejected_barriers.quote: [book-level] Stock phrases repeat word for word ('When Dawn, the rosy-fingered child of morning, appeared', 'struck the gray sea with their oars', 'loose the hawsers', 'through the livelong day ...', 'glad to have escaped death ...')
rejected_barriers.reason: These are GLOSSARY formulas and Butler's own repetitions, fixed on purpose. Repetition is not a comprehension failure, and every one was read correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: [book-level] 'should' for 'would', 'were for' / 'was for', 'made sure', 'misgave', 'wanted' for 'needed', 'neat milk', 'livelong'
rejected_barriers.reason: Each item is ruled on where it occurs. Only 'made sure' (¶36) is proposed (B09-01, optional), because its modern sense 'ensure' forces a re-read. The rest are dated but current, or their own sentence fixes them, and the reader read every one correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: [book-level] Sailing and farming vocabulary is left unexplained: hawsers, made fast, run before the gale, breakers, burden, laid out, whey, curdled, kids, yearlings, station, an auger with a wheel and strap
rejected_barriers.reason: These are current technical words or idioms, and the reader read each correctly in context. The auger clause was already adapted at the 2026-09-23 screening, and 'hawsers' and 'station' are kept by prior rulings.

rejected_barriers.quote: [book-level] Customs are assumed rather than explained
rejected_barriers.reason: The customs are Homer's. The brief rules out adding explanations Butler lacks.

rejected_barriers.quote: [book-level] The Cyclops is never said to have only one eye
rejected_barriers.reason: Homer's content (context note).

rejected_barriers.quote: [book-level] The Noman / no man trick relies on capitalization
rejected_barriers.reason: This is Butler's device, and it must keep working (task context). The text matches Butler, and how it sounds aloud is an audio or app matter.

rejected_barriers.quote: [book-level] A few pronouns point the wrong way on first reading (¶41, ¶32, ¶0)
rejected_barriers.reason: Each pronoun is Butler's, and the reader resolved all three with high confidence. See ¶41, ¶32 and ¶0.

rejected_barriers.quote: [book-level] The gods' motives at the end are unclear
rejected_barriers.reason: Homer's content (context note).

summary: Book 9 is already highly comprehensible. In all 44 paragraphs the blind reader's paraphrase matches Butler, and none of the 86 barriers is a misreading. The 9 barriers marked unsure are Homer's content and customs (the rite for the dead, suppliants, talents, the Cyclops's single eye, Zeus refusing the ram), Butler's own images and inconsistencies (the stubble fires, the rock thrown 'in front of' the ship yet near the rudder), or items already ruled on ('hawsers', and the auger clause adapted at the 2026-09-23 screening). The other 77 are pauses over names, GLOSSARY formulas and dated but transparent idioms, all recovered, mostly with high confidence. One false friend is worth an optional one-word repair: in 'we made sure it had been the death of us' (¶36), the modern sense 'ensure' forces a re-read, so it becomes 'felt sure', which is Butler's own phrase for that sense elsewhere in the poem. 'gobbets' and 'besmirched' (¶25) are current and exact, and the reader read both correctly ('besmirched' was restored by round-1 M-5), so both are kept. So are the prior rulings on 'subtlety', 'hawsers', 'livelong day', 'even so' and 'station', the 'should' and 'were for' idioms, and 'neat milk'. The Noman pun is Butler's and is untouched. Nothing is blocking or recommended.
